subject: money
topic: Most professional fund managers do not beat the market
angle: While most active funds underperformed passive benchmarks during the COVID-19 crisis and some evidence suggests a lack of skilled managers, funds with the highest Active Share significantly outperform their benchmarks both before and after expenses.
title: The Myth of the Skilled Manager

hooks.text: Who are you actually trusting with your future?
You assume managers are skilled. The evidence shows they often are not.
You are paying for a skill that might not exist.
A flickering screen in a dark office.

reveal.headline: High active share is linked to outperformance.
reveal.body: While many active funds underperform, those with the highest active share significantly outperform their benchmarks both before and after expenses. The evidence is mixed because results vary depending on the specific group of funds studied.

explain.headline: The evidence is mixed.
explain.body: Most active funds underperformed passive benchmarks during the 2020 covid-19 crisis. Nonindex funds with the lowest active share also underperform. However, specific characteristics like high active share are linked to outperformance.

matters.headline: Trust is not a strategy.
matters.body: That may be why simply hiring a manager is not enough. The data suggests that specific fund characteristics matter more than the mere existence of a professional.

example.headline: A spreadsheet on a desk.
example.body: You look at a list of names and fees. You assume the person at the top knows something you do not. You are looking for a skill that may not exist in the way you think.

verdict: The evidence is mixed, showing that while many active funds underperform, specific characteristics like high Active Share are linked to outperformance.
caveat: The findings vary significantly depending on the specific group of funds studied, such as those with high Active Share versus those with low Active Share.
caption:
Most people believe professional management guarantees better results.

Research shows mixed results: many active funds underperformed during the 2020 crisis, while those with the highest active share showed outperformance. The findings vary significantly depending on the specific group of funds studied.
